public_rationale: The core claim is that LLMs 'literally don't' reason and that this output came from retrieving a memorized answer. Both turn on what counts as reasoning, which Marcus does not define and researchers dispute. The mechanism behind one closed-model output cannot be seen from outside. A NAACL 2024 study cuts both ways: LLMs fall off sharply on altered versions of familiar tasks, which fits his picture, but they still show some abstract task-solving. Whether that counts as reasoning is a matter of definition, not evidence. The one checkable fact, that ChatGPT's answer was wrong, appears only in his own post.
limitations: Only one context study within the period was read in full. Later studies (2024-09, 2025-10) on altered riddles fall outside the target period.

our_interpretation: The claim has three parts: (a) ChatGPT's answer to Fraser's reworked riddle was wrong; (b) it produced the answer by retrieving the answer to the classic riddle; (c) LLMs in general 'literally don't' reason.
Part (a) rests on a screenshot in the post. The speaker's own post cannot be cited as evidence that he was right, and no independent record of that exact output was found.
Part (b) is a claim about the internal mechanism of a closed model on one output. Outsiders cannot observe that mechanism.
Part (c) depends on what counts as 'reasoning'. The speaker gives no definition, and researchers disagree on this point. So there is no ordinary plain reading that evidence could settle.
Target period: LLMs as of the post, from GPT-2 (2019) to July 2024, following the post's own framing.
criteria.support_condition: Would be supported if an accepted, operational definition of reasoning existed and independent tests showed LLMs of that era do none of it and only reproduce memorized answers to familiar problems.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Would be contradicted if, under an accepted definition of reasoning, independent tests or mechanistic analyses showed LLMs of that era performing genuine multi-step reasoning on novel variants.

evidence.excerpt: This suggests that while current LMs may possess abstract task-solving skills to an extent, they often also rely on narrow, non-transferable procedures for task-solving.
evidence.explanation: Shows that LLMs rely heavily on familiar patterns when tasks are altered, which fits Marcus's picture. The same paper finds some abstract task-solving ability, which cuts against 'literally don't reason'. Whether either finding counts as 'reasoning' depends on a definition.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: An agreed operational test of reasoning applied to LLMs of that era, or an independent reproduction plus mechanistic analysis of the specific riddle output.
